claims.claim: INaP and ICAN blockade have opposite effects on the relationship between network excitability and preBötC rhythmic activity.
claims.source: (1) INaP and ICAN blockade have opposite effects on the relationship between network excitability and preBötC rhythmic activity
claims.evidence: This prediction was experimentally tested and confirmed via optogenetic manipulations and pharmacological blockade, as described in the Results section and shown in Figures 4, 7, and 8.

claims.claim: INaP is essential for preBötC rhythmogenesis.
claims.source: (2) INaP is essential for preBötC rhythmogenesis
claims.evidence: This prediction was experimentally confirmed through complete blockade of INaP with TTX or riluzole, which eliminated rhythmic activity that could not be restored by optogenetic stimulation (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claims.claim: ICAN is essential for generating the amplitude of rhythmic output but not rhythm generation.
claims.source: (3) ICAN is essential for generating the amplitude of rhythmic output but not rhythm generation.
claims.evidence: This prediction was experimentally confirmed by pharmacological blockade of TRPM4 channels with 9-phenanthrol, which significantly reduced burst amplitude but had little effect on burst frequency (Figure 7).

claims.claim: The preBötC contains essential rhythmogenic neuronal circuits for mammalian breathing.
claims.source: The cellular and circuit biophysical mechanisms generating the breathing rhythm critical for life in mammals have been under investigation for decades without clear resolution (Richter and Smith, 2014; Del Negro et al., 2018; Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018). The roles of various transmembrane ionic currents in this process have received considerable attention, including our recent updated computational modeling (Phillips et al., 2019) of the biophysical mechanisms operating in the mammalian respiratory oscillator within the brainstem preBötzinger complex (preBötC), which contains essential rhythmogenic neuronal circuits.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature (Richter and Smith, 2014; Del Negro et al., 2018; Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018) and represents established scientific knowledge about the preBötC.

claims.claim: A subset of excitatory circuit neurons whose rhythmic bursting in the isolated preBötC in vitro is critically dependent on INaP forms an excitatory neuronal kernel for rhythm generation.
claims.source: The model proposes how these cellular-level mechanisms operating in excitatory circuits can underlie two critical functions of preBötC circuits: generation of the inspiratory rhythm and regulation of the amplitude of inspiratory population activity. In essence, the model advances the concepts that (1) a subset of excitatory circuit neurons, whose rhythmic bursting in the isolated preBötC in vitro is critically dependent on INaP, forms an excitatory neuronal kernel for rhythm generation
claims.evidence: This is a concept advanced by the computational model (Phillips et al., 2019) and tested experimentally in this study through pharmacological and optogenetic manipulations.

claims.claim: Excitatory synaptic drive from the rhythmogenic kernel population is critically amplified by ICAN activation in a recruited subset of preBötC excitatory neurons to generate overall population activity of sufficient amplitude to induce downstream excitatory circuits to produce inspiratory motor output.
claims.source: excitatory synaptic drive from the rhythmogenic kernel population is critically amplified by ICAN activation in a recruited subset of preBötC excitatory neurons to generate overall population activity of sufficient amplitude to induce downstream excitatory circuits to produce inspiratory motor output.
claims.evidence: This concept from the model is supported by experimental data showing that ICAN blockade significantly reduces burst amplitude while having minimal effect on rhythm generation (Figure 7).

claims.claim: Reducing gCAN (simulating ICAN blockade) strongly decreases population activity amplitude and has little effect on population bursting frequency under baseline conditions.
claims.source: Model simulations showing the relations between IApp, population burst frequency, and burst amplitude at different levels of gNaP and gCAN are displayed in Figure 1
claims.evidence: This prediction is shown in model simulations in Figure 1A-B and confirmed experimentally in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Reducing gNaP (simulating INaP blockade) decreases population-level bursting frequency and amplitude, reduces the frequency dynamic range, and at sufficiently low levels terminates rhythm generation.
claims.source: Model simulations showing the relations between IApp, population burst frequency, and burst amplitude at different levels of gNaP and gCAN are displayed in Figure 1
claims.evidence: This prediction is shown in model simulations in Figure 1C-D and confirmed experimentally in Figures 4 and 8.

claims.claim: ICAN blockade results in an upward shift and steeper slope in the frequency tuning curve that extends the frequency range at higher levels of population depolarization.
claims.source: ICAN block (gCAN reduction) more strongly decreases population activity amplitude in the model simulations than does INaP block and, in contrast to INaP block, has little effect on population bursting frequency under baseline conditions but strongly augments bursting frequency at higher levels of excitability. As such, ICAN block results in an upward shift and steeper slope in the frequency tuning curve that extends the frequency range at the higher levels of population depolarization, consistent with the experimental results (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by model simulations (Figure 1, Figure 8B) and confirmed by experimental data (Figure 7D, Figure 8C).

claims.claim: VgluT2-positive neurons in the preBötC express ChR2-EYFP fusion protein in somal membranes and neuronal processes.
claims.source: We verified Cre-driven ChR2-EYFP expression in VgluT2-positive tdTomato-labeled neurons within the preBötC region by two-photon microscopy in live neonatal mouse medullary slice (n=6) preparations in vitro, documenting heavy expression of the ChR2-EYFP fusion protein in processes and somal membranes of VgluT2-tdTomato-labeled neurons (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed and documented through two-photon microscopy imaging in live tissue preparations (Figure 2A).

claims.claim: Photostimulation of VgluT2-positive preBötC inspiratory neurons causes membrane depolarization in a laser-power-dependent manner.
claims.source: Summary data (n=12 neurons, mean ± SEM, Figure 2D) illustrates the laser-power-dependent ChR2-mediated depolarization of VgluT2-positive inspiratory preBötC neurons (4.73±0.24 mV at 0.5 mW, 6.01±0.21 mV at 1 mW, 8.55±0.29 mV at 2 mW, 10.21±0.34 mV at 3 mW, 11.13±0.3 mV at 4 mW, and 11.6±0.35 mV at 5 mW).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from identified neurons during photostimulation (Figure 2C-D).

claims.claim: The membrane depolarizations induced by different laser powers are significantly different (p<0.01 by ANOVA test).
claims.source: The membrane depolarizations are significantly different (p<0.01 by ANOVA test comparing these groups).
claims.evidence: This is determined by statistical analysis (ANOVA) of the experimental data on ChR2-mediated depolarization at different laser powers.

claims.claim: Bilateral photostimulation (0.25–2 mW) of the preBötC causes rapid and reversible increases of inspiratory burst frequency in a laser-power-dependent manner.
claims.source: Bilateral photostimulation (0.25–2 mW) of the preBötC caused rapid and reversible increases of inspiratory burst frequency in a laser-power-dependent manner (85±7% increase at 0.25 mW, 174±7% at 0.5 mW, 262±6% at 1 mW, 326±6% at 2 mW, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test, p<0.01 in all cases).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings from preBötC and XII nerves during bilateral photostimulation (Figure 3B-C).

claims.claim: Bilateral photostimulation causes a significant laser power-dependent decrease of burst amplitude of inspiratory preBötC population and inspiratory XII activity.
claims.source: Concurrently, there was a significant laser power-dependent decrease of burst amplitude of inspiratory preBötC population and inspiratory XII activity during photostimulation (8±2% decrease at 0.25 mW, 15±2% at 0.5 mW, 25±3% at 1 mW, 44±4% at 2 mW, p<0.01 in all cases by Wilcoxon signed rank test).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings during photostimulation experiments (Figure 3B-C).

claims.claim: After termination of laser illumination, an inhibition of rhythmicity follows and subsequently recovers to the control frequency.
claims.source: After termination of laser illumination, an inhibition of rhythmicity followed and subsequently recovered to the control frequency.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental recordings shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: TTX at low concentrations (5–20 nM) blocks INaP in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We first analyzed the pharmacological profile of block of INaP in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons with the INaP blockers tetrodotoxin citrate (TTX) at very low concentrations (5–20 nM, n=8) and also riluzole (5–20 µM, n=6) bath applied in the neonatal mouse medullary slice preparations
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp recordings showing TTX-sensitive INaP currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Riluzole (5–20 µM) blocks INaP in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons in a dose-dependent manner.
claims.source: We first analyzed the pharmacological profile of block of INaP in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons with the INaP blockers tetrodotoxin citrate (TTX) at very low concentrations (5–20 nM, n=8) and also riluzole (5–20 µM, n=6) bath applied in the neonatal mouse medullary slice preparations
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by voltage-clamp recordings showing riluzole-sensitive INaP currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: TTX reduced peak INaP by 36–63% at 5 nM, by 74–94% at 10 nM, and completely blocks INaP at 20 nM.
claims.source: TTX reduced peak INaP by 36–63% at 5 nM, by 74–94% at 10 nM, and completely blocks INaP at 20 nM.
claims.evidence: This is measured from voltage-clamp recordings of INaP in identified preBötC neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Riluzole reduced the peak INaP by 36–66% at 5 µM, by 82–95% at 10 µM, and completely blocked INaP at 20 µM.
claims.source: Riluzole reduced the peak INaP by 36–66% at 5 µM, by 82–95% at 10 µM, and completely blocked INaP at 20 µM.
claims.evidence: This is measured from voltage-clamp recordings of INaP in identified preBötC neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Endogenous burster inspiratory neurons have significantly higher gNaP/Cm (105.9±6.5 pS/pF) compared to non-endogenous burster inspiratory neurons (49.6±3.5 pS/pF) (p<0.05).
claims.source: In this dataset, there were five endogenous burster inspiratory neurons, which had significantly higher gNaP/Cm (105.9±6.5 pS/pF) compared to non-endogenous burster inspiratory neurons (49.6±3.5 pS/pF) (p<0.05 by non-parametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)
claims.evidence: This is measured from voltage-clamp recordings and is consistent with previous findings in neonatal rat slices (Koizumi and Smith, 2008).

claims.claim: Partial block of INaP (5–10 nM TTX, or 5–10 µM riluzole) gradually reduced XII inspiratory burst frequency, slightly reduced amplitude, and terminated inspiratory rhythmic bursting in almost all cases.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, partial block of INaP (5–10 nM TTX, or 5–10 µM riluzole) gradually reduced XII inspiratory burst frequency, slightly reduced amplitude, and terminated inspiratory rhythmic bursting in almost all cases (n=6/7 at 5 nM TTX, n=8/8 at 10 nM TTX, n=6/7 at 5 µM riluzole, n=8/8 at 10 µM riluzole).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings during pharmacological blockade of INaP (Figure 4A-B).

claims.claim: After rhythm termination by partial INaP block, bilateral photostimulation of the preBötC restored rhythmic bursting with voltage-dependent frequency control in all cases.
claims.source: In the cases where rhythmic bursting was terminated, after 30 min, we again bilaterally photostimulated the preBötC, which restored rhythmic bursting with voltage-dependent frequency control (0.25–2.0 mW) in all cases (n=14/14 with TTX, n=14/14 with riluzole).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental recordings showing rhythm restoration during photostimulation after partial INaP block (Figure 4B-C).

claims.claim: Under conditions of complete block of INaP (>30 min after either 20 nM TTX or 20 µM riluzole), bilateral sustained preBötC photostimulation could not reinitiate the inspiratory rhythm at any laser power ranging from 0.25 to 5 mW.
claims.source: Under conditions of complete block of INaP (>30 min after either 20 nM TTX or 20 µM riluzole), bilateral sustained preBötC photostimulation could not reinitiate the inspiratory rhythm at any laser power ranging from 0.25 to 5 mW (n=18/18 under TTX, n=11/11 under riluzole; Figures 4 and 5)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental recordings and power spectrum analyses showing absence of rhythmic activity after complete INaP block despite photostimulation (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claims.claim: After complete block of INaP, photostimulation induced only graded tonic spiking in preBötC neurons with progressive increases of laser power >1 mW, but no rhythmic bursting.
claims.source: Under conditions of complete block of INaP (>30 min after either 20 nM TTX or 20 µM riluzole), bilateral sustained preBötC photostimulation could not reinitiate the inspiratory rhythm at any laser power ranging from 0.25 to 5 mW (n=18/18 under TTX, n=11/11 under riluzole; Figures 4 and 5), but induced only graded tonic spiking in preBötC neurons with progressive increases of laser power >1 mW after block of INaP.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings and power spectrum analyses (Figures 5 and 6).

claims.claim: Power spectrum analyses of preBötC activity after complete INaP block show flat spectra with no rhythmic activity at each level of photostimulation-induced tonic activity.
claims.source: These spectral analyses of the recorded graded tonic activity after block of INaP indicated that there was no rhythmic activity at each level of the photostimulation-induced tonic activity in comparison to the control activity. In control conditions there is clear definition of spectral peaks for the fundamental and higher harmonic frequencies as given by the Fast Fourier Transform of the rectified preBötC activity signal. This power spectrum reflects the periodicity and (non-sinusoidal) shape of the bursts of population activity, but the spectrum is flat after block of INaP (Figure 5, n=5), reflecting a complete absence of rhythmic activity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by power spectrum analyses of preBötC population recordings (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Bath application of 9-phenanthrol (50 µM) significantly reduced the amplitude of inspiratory XII bursts (43±4% reduction, n=8, p<0.01) with little effects on burst frequency (1±1% increase, n=8, p=0.461).
claims.source: Bath application of 9-phenanthrol at a concentration proposed to be selective for TRPM4 (50 µM) to the rhythmically active slice preparations from VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2 neonatal mice (Figure 7A) significantly reduced the amplitude of inspiratory XII bursts (43±4% reduction, n=8, p<0.01 by Wilcoxon signed rank test), with little effects on burst frequency (1±1% increase, n=8, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p=0.461) in these slices
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings during TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Under TRPM4 block conditions, photostimulation caused a significant increase of inspiratory burst frequency compared to control conditions at a given laser power (0.25–2.0 mW).
claims.source: Under these TRPM4 block conditions (steady-state at >60 min after 9-phenanthrol application, Figure 7C), photostimulation caused a significant increase of inspiratory burst frequency compared to control conditions at a given laser power (0.25–2.0 mW, Figure 7D black lines, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.01 in all cases)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings during photostimulation under TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7C-D).

claims.claim: Under TRPM4 block conditions, photostimulation caused a significant laser-power-dependent decrease of burst amplitude compared to control.
claims.source: Under these TRPM4 block conditions (steady-state at >60 min after 9-phenanthrol application, Figure 7C), photostimulation caused a significant increase of inspiratory burst frequency compared to control conditions at a given laser power (0.25–2.0 mW, Figure 7D black lines, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.01 in all cases), accompanied by a significant laser-power-dependent decrease of burst amplitude compared to control (Figure 7D red lines, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.01 in all cases).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings during photostimulation under TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7C-D).

claims.claim: TRPM4 block significantly shifts the frequency tuning curve upward compared to control conditions.
claims.source: The relations between normalized inspiratory burst frequency and amplitude vs laser power summarized in Figure 7D (n=8 slice preparations, mean ± SEM plotted) show that TRPM4 block significantly shifts the frequency tuning curve upward compared to control conditions (black lines in Figure 7D, Wilcoxon signed rank test, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of frequency-laser power relationships under TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: Under baseline conditions of excitability, TRPM4 block does not alter burst frequency.
claims.source: Note that under baseline conditions of excitability, TRPM4 block does not alter burst frequency, and the upward shift in the frequency tuning curve is opposite to the shift seen with TTX or riluzole block of INaP.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing minimal frequency change at baseline (laser power = 0) after TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7A, D).

claims.claim: The ChR2 channel model can be parameterized to closely match experimental data on relations between laser power and membrane depolarization of preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons.
claims.source: We found that this biophysical model could be parameterized to closely match our experimental data on relations between laser power and membrane depolarization of identified preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the close match between model simulations and experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: TTX application was simulated by a direct reduction in gNaP.
claims.source: Therefore, as in previous work (Phillips and Rubin, 2019), TTX application was simulated by a direct reduction in gNaP
claims.evidence: This modeling approach is based on the known mechanism of action of TTX, which directly obstructs the Na+ pore (Hille, 2001).

claims.claim: Riluzole application was simulated by a hyperpolarizing shift in Vh1/2 and a reduction in the conductance of recurrent excitatory synaptic connections by 20 and 25%.
claims.source: Therefore, as in previous work (Phillips and Rubin, 2019), TTX application was simulated by a direct reduction in gNaP, while a hyperpolarizing shift in Vh1/2 and a reduction in the conductance of recurrent excitatory synaptic connections by 20 and 25% were used to simulate 5 µM and 10 µM riluzole application, respectively.
claims.evidence: This modeling approach is based on known pharmacological actions of riluzole: it shifts INaP inactivation dynamics in the hyperpolarizing direction (Hebert et al., 1994; Song et al., 1997; Ptak et al., 2005) and attenuates excitatory synaptic transmission (MacIver et al., 1996; Bellingham, 2011).

claims.claim: Model simulations show that TTX or riluzole block of INaP decreases the population-level bursting frequency and amplitude at each level of laser power.
claims.source: In agreement with the experimental results (Figure 4), the model simulations show that TTX or riluzole block of INaP decreases the population-level bursting frequency and amplitude at each level of laser power (Figure 8B–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by model simulations shown in Figure 8B and comparison with experimental data in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The downward shift in the amplitude vs laser power curve is larger with riluzole than TTX application due to the simulated off-target attenuating effects of riluzole on excitatory synaptic transmission.
claims.source: Due to the simulated off-target attenuating effects of riluzole on excitatory synaptic transmission, the downward shift in the amplitude vs laser power curve is larger with riluzole than TTX application (as also shown in Phillips and Rubin, 2019) as seen in the experimental data.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of model simulations and experimental data in Figure 8B-C, and is consistent with previous modeling work (Phillips and Rubin, 2019).

claims.claim: The model predictions are qualitatively consistent with the experimental data for major features of excitatory preBötC network behavior.
claims.source: Thus, the model predictions are qualitatively consistent with the experimental data for major features of excitatory preBötC network behavior.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the overall agreement between model simulations and experimental results shown in Figure 8 and throughout the Results section.

claims.claim: The VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2-EYFP triple transgenic mouse line was produced by crossing a VgluT2-Cre-tdTomato mouse with a Cre-dependent ChR2-EYFP mouse strain.
claims.source: The Cre-dependent triple transgenic mouse line VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2-EFYP, which expresses ChR2-EYFP fusion protein and tdTomato reporter fluorescent protein in VgluT2-positive neurons was used for optogenetic photostimulation experiments and in some experiments for imaging glutamatergic neurons for targeted whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiological recording from these neurons. This transgenic line was obtained by crossing the validated VgluT2-tdTomato line with the Cre-dependent optogenetic mouse strain (B6;129S-Gt[ROSA]26Sortm32(CAG-COP4*H134R/EYFP)Hze/J, the Jackson Laboratory).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methods used to generate the transgenic mouse line.

claims.claim: Rhythmically active medullary slice preparations were obtained from neonatal (postnatal day 3 [P3] to P8) VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2 mice of either sex.
claims.source: We performed optogenetic experiments combined with whole-cell patch-clamp or neural population electrophysiological recordings and pharmacological manipulations in rhythmically active in vitro medullary slice preparations (300–400 µm thick) from neonatal (postnatal day 3 [P3] to P8) VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2 mice of either sex.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental preparation used in the study.

claims.claim: The light-induced depolarization of VgluT2-positive preBötC neurons had fast kinetics, occurring within ~50 ms and recovery within ~150 ms after terminating illumination.
claims.source: The light-induced depolarization had fast kinetics, occurring within ~50 ms and recovery within ~150 ms after terminating illumination.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental recordings shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Bilateral photostimulation induced tonic activity in preBötC population recordings, which was of higher amplitude at higher laser power.
claims.source: Bilateral photostimulation also induced tonic activity in preBötC population recordings, which was of higher amplitude at higher laser power, but did not consistently induce tonic activities in XII nerve output.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the experimental recordings shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: XII burst amplitude and frequency always directionally mirrored preBötC glutamatergic population activity.
claims.source: Otherwise, XII burst amplitude and frequency always directionally mirrored preBötC glutamatergic population activity.
claims.evidence: This is observed throughout the experimental recordings (Figures 3, 4, 7).

claims.claim: In control experiments with rhythmic slice preparations from VgluT2-tdTomato, non-ChR2-expressing transgenic mice (n=6), there were no significant perturbations of frequency and amplitude as a function of laser power (0.25–2 mW).
claims.source: We note that in control experiments with rhythmic slice preparations from the VgluT2-tdTomato, non-ChR2-expressing transgenic mice (n=6), we tested for photo-induced perturbations of inspiratory burst frequency and amplitude, and confirmed that there were no significant perturbations of frequency and amplitude as a function of laser power (0.25–2 mW; ANOVA tests for frequency and burst amplitude, p=0.545 and 0.761, respectively).
claims.evidence: This control experiment confirms that the observed effects are due to ChR2 activation and not non-specific effects of laser illumination.

claims.claim: The INaP attenuation by TTX and riluzole blockers was not significantly different for endogenous burster and non-endogenous burster inspiratory neurons.
claims.source: However, the INaP attenuation by the blockers was not significantly different for these two groups (TTX: p=0.464 at 5 nM, p=0.982 at 10 nM, p=0.857 at 20 nM; riluzole: p=0.933 at 5 µM, p=0.4 at 10 µM, p=0.933 at 20 µM by non-parametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests).
claims.evidence: This is determined by statistical analysis of voltage-clamp data from different neuronal types.

claims.claim: The frequency tuning curves with TTX and riluzole shifted downward relative to control and more downwardly shifted with higher drug concentrations.
claims.source: The tuning curves with TTX and riluzole shifted downward relative to control (TTX 5 nM vs control, TTX 10 nM vs control, riluzole 5 µM vs control, riluzole 10 µM vs control; in all cases, p<0.01 by subsequent Tukey's HSD test), and more downwardly shifted with higher drug concentrations (Tukey's HSD test, TTX 5 nM vs TTX 10 nM, p<0.01; riluzole 5 µM vs riluzole 10 µM, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of the frequency-laser power relationships under different levels of INaP blockade (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: The frequency-laser power relations are not significantly different for the TTX and riluzole groups at equivalent concentrations.
claims.source: The frequency-laser power relations are not significantly different for the TTX and riluzole groups (Tukey's HSD test, p=0.927 for TTX 5 nM vs riluzole 5 µM; p=0.969 for TTX 10 nM vs riluzole 10 µM).
claims.evidence: This is determined by statistical analysis comparing the effects of TTX and riluzole on frequency tuning curves.

claims.claim: The curves obtained under riluzole were more significantly downward-shifted than those under TTX for amplitude vs laser power relationships.
claims.source: The curves obtained under riluzole were more significantly downward-shifted than those under TTX (TTX 5 nM vs riluzole 5 µM, p<0.01; TTX 10 nM vs riluzole 10 µM, p<0.01 by Tukey's HSD test).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of amplitude-laser power relationships (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: At the cellular level, current-clamp and voltage-clamp recordings confirmed the absence of neuronal rhythmic synaptic drive potentials/currents in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons after complete INaP block.
claims.source: At the cellular level, current-clamp and voltage-clamp recordings confirmed the absence of neuronal rhythmic synaptic drive potentials/currents in preBötC inspiratory glutamatergic neurons (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell recordings from preBötC neurons after complete INaP blockade (Figure 6).

claims.claim: INaP in preBötC glutamatergic neurons is critically involved in generating the inspiratory rhythm with a voltage-dependent frequency control mechanism in vitro.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that INaP in preBötC glutamatergic neurons is critically involved in generating the inspiratory rhythm with a voltage-dependent frequency control mechanism in vitro.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by the experimental results showing that complete INaP blockade eliminates rhythm generation and that partial blockade shifts the frequency tuning curve downward (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claims.claim: There are no apparent rhythmogenic mechanisms inherent within the excitatory network that can emerge at various levels of excitation after eliminating the INaP-dependent mechanisms.
claims.source: The results also indicate that there are no apparent rhythmogenic mechanisms inherent within the excitatory network that can emerge at various levels of excitation after eliminating the INaP-dependent mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is supported by power spectrum analyses showing no rhythmic activity after complete INaP blockade even with photostimulation (Figure 5).

claims.claim: ICAN/TRPM4 activation is not involved in rhythm generation under baseline conditions of network excitability.
claims.source: We note that our new measurements indicate that while ICAN /TRPM4 activation is not involved in rhythm generation under baseline conditions of network excitability, since inhibiting this current does not significantly affect the rhythm
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing minimal frequency change at baseline after TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7A, D).

claims.claim: Reducing ICAN/TRPM4 current shifts the frequency tuning curve at higher levels of network excitation because activation of this current augments excitatory synaptic interactions.
claims.source: we also show that reducing this current does shift the frequency tuning curve at higher levels of network excitation. This occurs because activation of this current augments excitatory synaptic interactions, which can affect network bursting frequency.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing upward shift in frequency tuning curve during photostimulation under TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7D) and is consistent with model predictions.

claims.claim: Endogenous activation of ICAN/TRPM4 is critically involved in generating the amplitude of population activity but not the rhythm.
claims.source: Our new experimental results confirm our previous experimental and modeling results indicating that endogenous activation of ICAN /TRPM4 is critically involved in generating the amplitude of population activity but not the rhythm, which is also consistent with results from a genetic knockdown study of TRPM4 channels in preBötC neurons in vivo (Picardo et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing significant amplitude reduction with minimal frequency change after TRPM4 blockade (Figure 7), and is consistent with previous studies (Picardo et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Activation of ICAN is largely due to synaptically activated sources of neuronal Ca2+ flux such that ICAN contributes to the excitatory inspiratory drive potential and regulates inspiratory burst amplitude by augmenting the excitatory synaptic current.
claims.source: The correspondence between the experimental data and model predictions supports the concept in the model that activation of ICAN is largely due to synaptically activated sources of neuronal Ca2+ flux such that ICAN contributes to the excitatory inspiratory drive potential and regulates inspiratory burst amplitude by augmenting the excitatory synaptic current.
claims.evidence: This concept is supported by the agreement between model predictions and experimental data on the effects of ICAN blockade (Figures 7, 8).

claims.claim: INaP is involved, to a smaller degree than ICAN, in generating the amplitude of rhythmic population activity at a given level of excitatory network excitation.
claims.source: Our data also show that INaP is involved, to a smaller degree, in generating the amplitude of rhythmic population activity at a given level of excitatory network excitation. This is due to the subthreshold activation of INaP and its voltage-dependent amplification of synaptic drive
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data showing amplitude reductions with INaP blockade, though smaller than with ICAN blockade (Figures 4, 8).

claims.claim: Application of riluzole affected population amplitude much more than application of TTX.
claims.source: indeed, application of riluzole, which is thought to impact synaptic transmission, affected population amplitude much more than application of TTX (Figures 4 and 8).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of amplitude effects in Figures 4 and 8.

claims.claim: ICAN activation in a subpopulation of preBötC excitatory neurons is critically involved in amplifying synaptic drive from a subset of neurons whose rhythmic bursting is critically dependent on INaP.
claims.source: In general, our results support the concept from our original model that ICAN activation in a subpopulation of preBötC excitatory neurons is critically involved in amplifying synaptic drive from a subset of neurons whose rhythmic bursting is critically dependent on INaP . This latter subpopulation forms the kernel for rhythm generation in vitro.
claims.evidence: This concept is supported by the overall agreement between model predictions and experimental results on the distinct roles of INaP and ICAN.

results.result: A prior computational model (Phillips et al., 2019) proposed that INaP and ICAN are key biophysical factors generating inspiratory rhythm and burst pattern, respectively, in the preBötC respiratory oscillator in vitro.
results.evaluation: C1 accurately describes the hypothesis from the cited prior work (Phillips et al., 2019). This is a statement about what was proposed in a previous study and is appropriately supported by citation.

results.result: INaP and ICAN blockade have opposite effects on the relationship between network excitability and preBötC rhythmic activity. Partial INaP blockade shifts the frequency tuning curve downward and reduces amplitude, while ICAN blockade shifts the frequency tuning curve upward at elevated excitability but does not affect baseline frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C8-C10, C14-C15, C22-C23, C27-C31, and C45-C47 collectively demonstrate opposite effects of INaP and ICAN blockade on frequency-excitability relationships through both model predictions and experimental validation. The experimental data (Figures 4, 7, 8) with appropriate statistical tests (p<0.01) strongly support these opposing effects, confirming model predictions.

results.result: INaP is essential for preBötC rhythmogenesis in vitro. Complete pharmacological blockade of INaP with TTX or riluzole eliminates rhythmic activity that cannot be restored by optogenetic stimulation, and no alternative rhythmogenic mechanisms emerge at various levels of excitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C17-C21, C24-C26, C48-C50, C65, and C78 provide converging evidence from pharmacological characterization (voltage-clamp), network recordings, power spectrum analyses, and optogenetic rescue experiments. Complete INaP blockade (20 nM TTX or 20 µM riluzole) eliminated rhythm in all cases (n=18/18 TTX, n=11/11 riluzole), with flat power spectra confirming absence of rhythmic activity despite photostimulation up to 5 mW. This strongly supports the essential role of INaP in rhythm generation.

results.result: ICAN is essential for generating the amplitude of rhythmic output but not rhythm generation. TRPM4 blockade significantly reduces burst amplitude (43±4% reduction) with minimal effect on baseline frequency, but shifts the frequency tuning curve upward at elevated excitability levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C31, and C51-C54 demonstrate through pharmacological blockade with 9-phenanthrol (50 µM, n=8) that ICAN/TRPM4 is critical for amplitude but not baseline rhythm generation. The experimental data show significant amplitude reduction (p<0.01) with no significant frequency change at baseline (p=0.461), consistent with model predictions and prior studies (Picardo et al., 2019).

results.result: A VgluT2-tdTomato-ChR2-EYFP triple transgenic mouse line was generated and validated for optogenetic manipulation of preBötC glutamatergic neurons. ChR2-EYFP is expressed in VgluT2-positive neurons, and photostimulation causes laser-power-dependent membrane depolarization with fast kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C38-C40 describe the generation and validation of the transgenic mouse line with appropriate methods (two-photon microscopy, whole-cell recordings, n=12 neurons from 4 preparations). The laser-power-dependent depolarization is well-characterized (4.73±0.24 mV at 0.5 mW to 11.6±0.35 mV at 5 mW) with significant differences confirmed by ANOVA (p<0.01). Control experiments (C43) confirm specificity.

results.result: Bilateral photostimulation of preBötC glutamatergic neurons causes rapid, reversible, laser-power-dependent increases in inspiratory burst frequency and decreases in burst amplitude. XII motor output mirrors preBötC population activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C41-C43 demonstrate dose-dependent effects of photostimulation (n=31 preparations) with appropriate statistics (Wilcoxon tests, p<0.01). Frequency increases ranged from 85±7% at 0.25 mW to 326±6% at 2 mW, while amplitude decreased from 8±2% to 44±4%. Control experiments without ChR2 (n=6) showed no effects (p=0.545 and 0.761), confirming specificity.

results.result: A biophysical ChR2 channel model was parameterized to match experimental data on laser-power-dependent neuronal depolarization. Model simulations incorporating pharmacological manipulations of INaP and ICAN show qualitative agreement with experimental results for major features of preBötC network behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 and C80 demonstrate that the computational model, extended with a four-state Markov ChR2 channel model, closely matches experimental data (Figure 8A). The model correctly predicts the directional effects of TTX, riluzole, and ICAN blockade on frequency and amplitude tuning curves, with appropriate incorporation of known pharmacological mechanisms from the literature.

results.result: INaP contributes to burst amplitude generation to a smaller degree than ICAN, through subthreshold activation and voltage-dependent amplification of synaptic drive. Riluzole affects amplitude more than TTX due to off-target effects on excitatory synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 and C66-C69 are supported by experimental data showing differential amplitude effects of riluzole vs TTX (Figures 4, 8), consistent with known pharmacological actions of riluzole on synaptic transmission (MacIver et al., 1996; Bellingham, 2011). Model simulations incorporating 20-25% synaptic conductance reduction match experimental observations.

results.result: The model proposes that a subset of excitatory neurons with INaP-dependent rhythmogenic properties forms a rhythmogenic kernel, and ICAN activation in a recruited subpopulation amplifies synaptic drive from this kernel to generate population activity amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C57, and C79 describe conceptual predictions from the model that are indirectly supported by the overall agreement between model and experimental data. However, direct experimental evidence for distinct neuronal subpopulations with these specific properties is not provided. C79 explicitly states this prediction requires experimental testing (e.g., dynamic multicellular Ca2+ imaging).

results.result: The current study addresses conflicting prior results on the role of INaP in preBötC rhythm generation. The results contradict the hypothesis of Pace et al., 2007 that INaP blockade affects rhythm by reducing excitability rather than affecting essential rhythmogenic mechanisms, demonstrating that optogenetic stimulation cannot restore rhythm after complete INaP blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 provide appropriate context from prior literature and directly test the hypothesis from Pace et al., 2007. The experimental results (C65) showing inability to restore rhythm after complete INaP blockade despite photostimulation (n=18/18 TTX, n=11/11 riluzole) provide strong evidence against the alternative hypothesis and support the essential role of INaP.

results.result: Non-uniform drug penetration in thick slices due to passive diffusion, combined with spatial organization of rhythmogenic neurons near the center of the preBötC network, may explain conflicting results in prior studies using thick slices where INaP blockade primarily affected amplitude rather than frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 present reasonable mechanistic explanations for discrepancies in the literature, supported by general biophysical principles (drug diffusion) and prior observations (C72: Baertsch et al., 2019). However, these remain inferences and predictions rather than directly tested hypotheses in the current study. The explanation is plausible but requires experimental validation.

results.result: In more intact brainstem preparations, INaP blockers do not disrupt rhythm generation due to more complex synaptic interactions including inhibitory circuits. Modeling predicts network states where inspiratory rhythm may be highly dependent on INaP in more intact systems, requiring further experimental testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 appropriately cite prior experimental (Smith et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2009b) and modeling studies (Rubin and Smith, 2019; Phillips and Rubin, 2019) showing different roles of INaP in more intact preparations. C77 appropriately identifies this as a prediction requiring experimental validation. The claims accurately represent the state of knowledge.

results.result: The preBötC contains essential rhythmogenic neuronal circuits for mammalian breathing.
results.evaluation: C5 represents well-established knowledge in the field, appropriately supported by citations to multiple authoritative reviews (Richter and Smith, 2014; Del Negro et al., 2018; Ramirez and Baertsch, 2018). This provides necessary background context.

results.result: INaP attenuation by TTX and riluzole was not significantly different between endogenous burster and non-endogenous burster inspiratory neurons.
results.evaluation: C44 reports statistical comparisons (Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests) showing no significant differences in INaP blockade between neuronal subtypes at all concentrations tested (p>0.4 in all cases). This is a straightforward negative result appropriately analyzed.

results.result: The agreement between model predictions and experimental results advances understanding of neuronal and circuit biophysical mechanisms generating rhythm and amplitude of inspiratory activity in the preBötC in vitro and demonstrates the predictive power of the model.
results.evaluation: C81 is a summary conclusion supported by the overall agreement between model simulations and experimental data demonstrated throughout the Results section, particularly in the comprehensive comparisons shown in Figure 8. The claim appropriately reflects the scope and significance of the findings.
